tests.description: Timed check on The Roman Conquest of Britain

questions.question: Q: Why did Claudius invade Britain in 43 CE?
questions.correctAnswer: Claudius needed a military victory to legitimise his position as emperor. Conquering Britain, which Caesar had only raided, would give him prestige and secure his political authority.

questions.question: Q: What caused Boudica's revolt?
questions.correctAnswer: After her husband died, Romans seized Iceni lands, flogged Boudica and assaulted her daughters. This brutality combined with heavy taxation triggered widespread rebellion.

questions.question: Q: How far did Romanisation change British culture?
questions.correctAnswer: Significantly in the south and east with towns, villas, baths and roads transforming daily life. But in the north and west Celtic culture persisted. Romanisation was uneven across Britain.

tests.name: Exam-Style Practice
tests.description: Short-answer practice on The Roman Conquest of Britain

questions.question: Q: What was the purpose of Hadrian's Wall?
questions.correctAnswer: To mark and defend the frontier, control movement and trade, and project Roman power. It was as much a customs and administrative barrier as a military defence.

questions.question: Q: Why did some Britons cooperate with Rome?
questions.correctAnswer: Cooperation brought wealth, status and access to Roman goods. Client kings retained local power while gaining the benefits of empire.

questions.question: Full-Mark Response How far did the Roman conquest benefit Britain? (15 marks) <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: The Roman conquest brought significant material benefits to Britain, but these were unevenly distributed and came at considerable cost in lost independence and cultural disruption. Benefits included roads connecting communities, towns with baths and forums, villas with Mediterranean-style comfort, expanded trade, and writing, coinage and Roman law creating a more complex society. Wealthy Britons who built villas enjoyed higher living standards. However, benefits were unequal — the elite gained most while ordinary farmers saw little improvement. The conquest was brutal — Boudica's revolt showed Roman savagery, and Celtic sacred sites were destroyed. Taxes extracted wealth for Rome. Slavery extracted people. Romanisation was not universally desired. In the north beyond Hadrian's Wall, Roman benefits barely reached. Overall, material advances primarily benefited the elite and cooperative elements, while costs — loss of independence, heavy taxation, cultural erosion and brutality — were borne most heavily by those with least power.
